## Original problem (task)
[01274f41553299e7] (h005.task.v1)
I share a flat with two friends. We keep arguing about ordinary household chores. Sometimes we agree on who will do something, but later we disagree about what the agreement meant. Our work schedules change, and one friend has started avoiding the conversations. What should I do?

## Selected input account (p.objection.0)

BODY
This begins the account fresh: a previous account slot was selected, but no text of it is visible to me, so nothing here builds on or revises earlier claims.

The chore fights look like three separate faults stacked on top of each other, and it helps to keep them apart.

**1. Agreements that aren't really agreements.** 'We agree on who will do something, but later disagree about what the agreement meant' is the signature of under-specified commitments — no settled what, when, or what-done-looks-like. Three people can leave the same conversation holding three different agreements, each honestly believed. The remedy is boring but effective: agreements get written down somewhere all three can see, in checkable terms ('kitchen counters wiped and dishwasher started by 9pm'), not in good-intention terms.

**2. An allocation that can't survive the schedules.** A fixed rota assumes stable weeks. With shifting work schedules, any static division decays within a fortnight, and every failure reopens negotiation at the worst moment — at the scene of an unwashed pan. Two robust alternatives: a short weekly re-deal (ten minutes, same time each week, allocate the coming week against actual schedules), or trigger-based rules ('first one home starts dinner'). Either moves renegotiation out of the moment of failure.

**3. A participant opting out — and this one matters most.** One friend avoiding the conversations means the conversation itself has become a cost. The material doesn't say why: conflict-aversion, feeling out-voted two-against-one, a sense the process is rigged, or something unrelated that the chore talks have become a proxy for. What I'd try: approach them one-on-one, not about any specific chore, ask what would make the household talks easier, and offer an asynchronous channel (the shared written record doubles as this) — avoidant people often engage readily in writing.

Conjectures I'm holding loosely: the disagreement about meaning may sometimes be re-litigation — someone reopening a deal they regret — rather than genuine ambiguity; written specificity helps in both cases, so it doesn't change the advice. The avoidance may also be an early symptom of someone drifting toward moving out; worth bearing in mind, not worth acting on preemptively.

What I'd actually do, in order: (a) propose one short meeting framed explicitly as fixing the system, not reviewing who failed last week; (b) there, agree a short list of standards and pick one allocation mechanism from point 2; (c) set up the written record in the group chat or on the fridge; (d) separately and privately, have the one-on-one conversation with the avoidant friend; (e) after two or three weekly cycles, revisit whatever keeps failing rather than treating any arrangement as final.

One caution against my own remedy: a written chore system can curdle into bureaucracy and relocate the fight from the sink to the wording of the list. Guard against it by keeping the record minimal and treating it as revisable, not law.

Unanswered: whether the three of you actually share minimum standards (a standards gap needs negotiation of the standards themselves, possibly with trades across domains), and what the avoidant friend is really avoiding. Those two unknowns determine whether this is a logistics problem or a relationship problem wearing a logistics costume.
